## Overview

This blog post explores the ["Leading at
Scale"](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch06.html) chapter from
[*Software Engineering at Google*](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book),
written by Ben Collins-Sussman and edited by Riona MacNamara. The previous
chapter, "How to Lead a Team," focused on leading one team. This chapter goes
a step further and looks at what changes when a leader is in charge of many
teams at once. At that level, a leader cannot be involved in every technical
detail anymore, so their job becomes making good decisions, building teams
that can work without them, and protecting their own time and energy. The
chapter organizes this advice around three ideas: **Always Be Deciding**,
**Always Be Leaving**, and **Always Be Scaling**. Even as students, these ideas
apply to us, since we often lead small parts of our team projects and need to
make sure the project does not fall apart when one person is busy or
unavailable.

## Summary

### Always Be Deciding
Managing a team of teams means making more decisions all the time, and higher level decisions at that. Jobs become about high-level
strategy, as compared to solving any one single task. Additionally, you should always be considering trade-offs. Some trade offs are
simple: "working on one project means postponing another". However, other times, the trade-offs have unforseen results or consequences
that nobody can predict or prepare for.

#### Identify the Blinders
When approaching a problem, there's likely a group of people already investing work into the problem, sometimes for so long that they've
become 'blind' to the status quo. This is where someone with a fresh perspective on the problem has an advantage, since they're able to
look at the problem in a way it hasn't previously been looked at.

### Always Be Leaving
At face value, "Always Be Leaving" appears to be terrible advice. But actually, this is a famous quote from Bharat Mediratta, who is a
former Google engineering director! The quote means that solving an ambiguous problem isn't exactly your job, but the organization's job,
and your job is to get the organization to solve it by itself, even without your presence.

Being a successful leader means building an organization capable of solving a problem on its own. Immediately, the bus factor might come
back to mind. A successful organization can work around this and become self-sufficient and self-driving. If you as a leader can disappear,
or get sick, or go on vacation, and the team will continue to work, the team is on its path to being self-sufficient.

One way to break down the tasks or problems a team is facing is by dividing them into subproblems: smaller tasks or problems that can be
handled by a small team or even one single individual. When put together, these teams can work on each individual subproblem at a high level
of efficiency. However, subproblems can change, and rigid team boundaries won't change to meet the changing problems. Walking a fine line
between "too rigid" and "too vague" is the key to success.

### Always Be Scaling
When a team is handling a difficult problem, a pattern emerges: analysis, struggle, traction, reward. Typically, however, a team will not
get more members as it gets more problem. This leads to a 'compression' stage needing added to the pattern, where a team needs to scale a
problem to fit within half the size AND half the time.

Leadership is extremely stressful - and higher-leadership roles only force more reactive acting as opposed to granding proactive opportunity.
More time spent being reactive causes attention to fall to urgent problems, but not important problems. Being a leader means that you need to
perform work on the problems that ONLY the leader (you) is capable of.

#### Key Techniques
Delegate - Pass urgent tasks to other leaders and people who are capable of doing those tasks.
Schedule - Regularly block out hours and timeslots to sit and work on important, but NOT urgent tasks. This will save them from BECOMING urgent.
Track - Make a system for task-tracking, and make sure it works and works well. It will allow you to identify those important tasks you may not see.


## Action Items
Start - Scheduling work time, tracking problems, and delegating tasks to people who can do them.
Stop - Working without focus, ignoring important tasks for urgent ones, and ignoring forms of task planning
Continue - Monitoring work with teams, consdering the bus factor, and maintaining efficiency


::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" title="Open-Source Tool for Software Engineers" collapse="false"}

Our team built `busfactor`, a Python command-line tool that reads a Git
repository's history and finds the files that only one person has ever worked
on. It also estimates the team's bus factor, which is how many people would
have to leave before most of the files have nobody left who worked on them.
This connects to the chapter's idea of "Always Be Leaving," since a good
leader builds a team that does not depend on any single person. You can view
the project here: [busfactor on GitHub](https://github.com/Jsharsh33v/busfactor).

:::
